newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish economic boom seen continuing into 1999-govt.
newsitem.headline: Irish economic boom seen continuing into 1999-govt.

text.p: Ireland's economy is likely to continue its high levels of growth into 1999, a government report said on Friday.

The report, entitled "Ireland - Convergence Programme 1997 to 1999", is part of an EU-wide programme to facilitate multi-lateral surveillance of economic policies ahead of the third stage of European economic and monetary union in 1999.
"The policies set out in this Convergence Programme have been formed in the context of an expected continuation of strong economic growth and price stability," the report said.
It forecast annual economic growth averaging 4.75 percent during the period 1997 to 1999, with inflation averaging 2.1 percent.
Total employment is forecast to grow by 114,000 or 2.9 percent per annum over the three years with non-agricultural employment expected to rise by about 122,000 or 3.4 percent per annum.

The report said domestic demand will continue to provide the major contribution to the overall growth rate, although at a somewhat reduced pace, reflecting moderation in employment growth and a reduced rate of increase in investment.
It said the contribution made by net exports will increase reflecting an improving international environment.

The Convergence Programme was underpinned, it said, by the low inflation and pay elements of a three-year national programme, Partnership 2000, agreed between the government, employers and trade unions.

Continued prudent fiscal management and moderate income developments have kept the budget deficit below 2.0 percent of GDP in the past three years and this approach will be maintained over the next three years, it said.
It expects the General Government Deficit to be contained at no more than 1.5 percent of GDP, which it said would keep the underlying debt/GDP ratio on a downward path at a satisfactory pace.
The report is based on the latest economic forecasts for Ireland's trading partners from the European Commission and other international agencies.
Based on an assumption that world trade is expected to expand at 7.0 percent per annum, Ireland's export markets are seen growing by 6.25 percent annually, the report said.
Gross Domestic Product (GDP) growth in both the EU and the OECD is expected to average 2.5 percent and inflation rates are assumed to continue to converge.
